Program: Unconference 1: A “Garden of Forking Paths” or of “Apples and Oranges”?
Topic: When a large number of researchers is asked to analyze the same dataset to address a shared research question, results often show substantial heterogeneity between analysts. This heterogeneity has been documented in several “many-analyst studies”, and is usually attributed to arbitrary decisions in data analysis (the so-called “Garden of Forking Paths”), which seems to be the reason behind the variance in study outcomes and conclusions. In this Unconference, we would like to discuss whether such heterogeneity truly reflects noise emerging from arbitrary analysis decisions, or whether different researchers were in fact addressing different biological questions (i.e. “comparing Apples and Oranges”).
Outline: The session will start with an introductory note on how heterogeneity in research findings can be explained as originating from multiple sources of error, one of which is the uncertainty of how to best analyze the data. We will then proceed to a specific example, which illustrates that truly arbitrary analysis decisions have surprisingly little effect on the outcome, and that most of the disagreement in conclusions results from researchers implicitly asking different questions, often without being aware of this. This will serve as a starting point for an open discussion on the generality of these insights and their implications.
Audience: Everyone is welcome and likely to benefit, regardless of statistical background. Researchers with expertise in statistics, meta-analysis, and philosophy of science are particularly encouraged to attend.

Program: Hackathon 1: Rally support for Open Science in Ecology & Evolution
Topic: Help promote SORTEE to a wide and diverse audience! In this hackathon, we’ll use email and social media templates to invite your colleagues and peers to connect to SORTEE. Together, the hackathon participants’ extended network will thus rally support for Open Science in Ecology & Evolution.
Outline:
We will come together as a community and work towards our shared goal of rallying support for more Open, Reliable and Transparent (ORT) research in Ecology & Evolution. By becoming a SORTEE member and inviting potential new members, you help expand SORTEE’s community, so SORTEE can be more efficient in advocating for and training people in ORT.</br>
During the hackathon, we will do three activities towards this goal:</br>
(1) Use our committee’s new outreach email and social media templates to invite your colleagues to SORTEE.</br>
(2) Expand SORTEE's social media networks, to invite diverse groups of people to connect to SORTEE on LinkedIn and BlueSky, via a short tutorial.</br>
(3) Open discussion on how to best pitch SORTEE to others.</br>
Join and meet each other! Boosting your motivation to keep working towards Open Science.
Audience: Everyone. Anyone interested in Open Science and willing to help expand SORTEE’s community is welcome.

Program: Unconference 2: Establishing guidelines for research integrity in macroecology and macroevolution
Facilitators: Joseph Tobias, Bethany Allen, Alex Pigot, Will Pearse
Topic: Research quality in macroecology, macroevolution and One Health may be undermined by inappropriate research practices, yet pre-registration of research proposals in these high-impact fields is almost non-existent. This session will explore whether pre-registration could improve research transparency, rigour and integrity in non-experimental macro-scale research, and if so what form it should take. The goal is to co-create an outline of guidelines that could be developed and published to promote pre-registration and related practices in fields often considered to be outside the scope of pre-registration.
Outline:
0–15 mins: Introduction
15–45 mins: Break-out session 1 “challenges and opportunities” (2 groups A and B)
45–60 mins: Summary and discussion of goals
60–100 mins: Break out session 2 “planning the guidelines” (2 groups A and B)
100–120 mins: Wrap up and suggestions for next steps

Program: Hackathon 2: EcoEvo SORTEE ReproHack: Reproducibility Hackathon of Recent Research in Ecology & Evolution
Topic: The session's main theme is to to learn about reproducible methods by attempting to reproduce a recently published EcoEvo journal article. The goals will be to identify instructions for reproducing the analysis and figures, attempt to follow them, and reflect on the exercise. Participants will be placed in groups of mixed experience levels and will be assisted by the two instructors.
Outline:
The session will run in 3 parts:</br>
1) A short introductory lecture with tips and tricks on how to attempt to reproduce a paper ;</br>
2) Attendees will break off in small groups, each attempting to reproduce a different paper and filling up a qualitative openness score sheet ;</br>
3) We will reconvene and read together the score sheets. Participants will be encouraged to continue with the reproducibility exercise after the hackathon.
Audience: This hackathon is open to anyone acquainted with the basics of running code on their computer (for example, opening and running a script in RStudio). We encourage anyone interested in the reproducibility of the code they encounter or submit in journals to join us. We will aim to balance groups between experienced and inexperiences coders.

Program: Workshop 1: Using and extending data standards in wildlife disease ecology
Topic: The session’s goal is to familiarize participants with the Wildlife Disease Data Standard through hands-on activities. Participants will be able to determine when the standard is applicable, set up data collection instruments, convert existing data to be standard-compliant, and use the standard and accompanying R package to validate data. Ultimately, participants will gain a deeper understanding of how to create FAIR datasets.
Outline:
The workshop will last 60 mins and be broken into 3 sections. </br>
First, introduce challenges to data re-use in disease ecology and basic concepts around using data standards (5 mins);</br>
second, introduce the wildlife disease data standard (10 min);</br>
third, use the Wildlife Disease Data Standard and associated R package in hands-on activities relevant to different components of the research data life cycle (45 mins).
Audience: Basic proficiency with excel or other spreadsheet software. Ability to install packages, load data, and run scripts in R. Ability to download or clone a repository from Github.

Program: Unconference 3: Researchers experiences with Registered Reports in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
Facilitators: Joel Pick, Marija Purgar, Kevin Bairos-Novak, Shinichi Nakagawa,  Losia Lagisz
Topic: Registered reports are a key tool in addressing the replication crisis by increasing transparency, addressing questionable research practices, and reducing research waste and publication bias. However, their uptake in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology is extremely low for several reasons, including lack of awareness and misconceptions. We aim to address these issues in an open discussion with researchers experienced with Registered Reports in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology.
Outline: We will host an open discussion with a panel of researchers in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology that have used registered reports. We aim to inform researchers about registered reports, and discuss some actionable goals to try and increase registered reports with Ecology and Evolutionary Biology. We will guide the discussion to key topics such as ‘how was the experience of submitting a registered report‘, ‘what problems did you encounter’, ‘how can we improve the experience of submitting registered reports’.

Program: Hackathon 3: Database of open science policies for major national funding agencies
Topic: National funding agencies have a lot of leverage to change research practices, not only in E&E, but in all fields of research, and many have adopted policies that encourage or require open science practices. Previous efforts by SORTEE members to document and centralize the data and code policies of E&E journals have produced publicly available databases and associated papers for use by (meta)researchers but centralized information on funder policies is lacking. This hackathon will adopt a similar approach, focusing on funders rather than journals, to address a critical information gap, which will enable researchers from around the globe to better understand their responsibilities when accepting funding; funding agencies to compare and align their policies to those of other funders; and metaresearchers to monitor changes in open science policies over time and across jurisdictions.
Outline:
Participants will be introduced to the purpose and aim of the hackathon at the start of the session (short presentation by the facilitator);</br>
the methods will be explained, including data collection via a Google form, task assignment for each participant, data validation procedures, and post-hackathon communication;</br>
participants will then be introduced to the data collection methods via a live demonstration. Data collection will begin during the hackathon and continue afterwards (estimated 2-3h of post-hackathon work per participant). The database resulting from the hackathon will be shared publicly, with the aim of producing a paper providing a snapshot of open science policy status for national funding agencies from groups such as the G7, G20, OECD.
Audience: Everyone. All participants are welcome to join the hackathon. No specific expertise is required.

Program: Plenary Talk by Simine Vazire: Where are the Self-Correcting Mechanisms in Science?
Topic: We often hear the self-correcting mechanisms in science invoked as a reason to trust science, but it is not always clear what these mechanisms are. Some quality control mechanisms, such as peer review for journals, have been found not to provide much of a safeguard against invalid claims. Instead, I argue that we should look for visible signs of a scientific community's commitment to self-correction. These signs include transparency in the research and peer review process, investment in error detection and quality control, and an emphasis on calibration rather than popularization. We should trust scientific claims more to the extent that they were produced by communities that have these hallmarks of credibility. Fields that are more transparent, rigorous, and calibrated should earn more trust. Metascience can provide scientists and the public with valuable information in assessing the credibility of scientific fields.
Outline: 40 min presentation, 20 min questions

Program: Workshop 3: The Confound Hour: Promoting Open Discussions of Scientific Failure at Scientific Conferences
Topic:
Scientific meetings celebrate scientific achievement: famous keynote speakers, beautiful results, award ceremonies. This focus is exciting and invigorating, but glosses over the many failures, mistakes, and rejections that typically lead to scientific success. By creating space within scientific meetings for open conversation about failure we can increase scientific transparency and resilience.
By attending this workshop, we hope attendees will:
1) Recognize that the experience of failure in science is universal and essential for insight and growth.
2) Feel more comfortable acknowledging and discussing struggle and failure with colleagues and trainees.
3) Have a toolbox of activities and games for promoting open discussions of scientific failure within their own communities and events.
Outline: In this workshop, we will share the materials that we have used at a large international scientific conference during the past four years (Society for Neuroscience: 2021-2024) to promote open discussions of scientific failure, including formal storytelling, individual and interactive games, and confessionals (overview: https://doi.org/10.1523/ENEURO.0524-24.2024). For each activity, we will provide the rationale and practical guidance regarding logistics and usage. We will also demonstrate a few of the games, allowing workshop participants to experience open discussions of scientific failure in a professional setting. The end of the workshop will center on brainstorming how participants can best adapt the activities to their own communities or local events.

Outline: A presentation broken up into key topics (e.g., "Code and data sharing" or "Preprints"). For each, the facilitators will explain what it means, the motivation for doing it, and give links to useful resources (papers, tools like EcoEvoRxiv, Dryad, etc.)
Audience: A session dedicated to people new to open science practices but everybody is welcome to attend!

Program: Unconference 4: What do LLMs mean for open science?
Topic: The last three years have seen the rapid uptake of large language models (LLMs) across nearly every facet of the scientific research process. There has been much debate over the pros and cons of this development in general, but comparatively less about the implications for open science specifically. In this Unconference session, we will lead a discussion on the potential challenges and opportunities for open, reliable, and transparent research in the face of widespread use of LLMs.
Outline: This session will begin with some open questions querying the possible impacts of LLMs on open science - what are the possible ways they can support our mission, and what are the foreseeable risks that may emerge from their use? We will frame the remainder of the discussion around the answers to these prompts, focusing on the areas that attendees believe are the most important points for discussion. To end the session, we will ask what (if anything) SORTEE and other similar groups should be doing to navigate the shifting open science ecosystem in the LLM era.
Audience: This session is open to everyone, including those with strong views on either side of this debate.

Program: Hackathon 4: Evaluating FAIR principles and uncertainty in mechanistic models from ecology and evolution
Topic: The main goal of the hackathon is to develop a framework for evaluating mechanistic models’ openness, transparency, reproducibility, and methods of assessing model precision and accuracy. This framework will subsequently be applied to studies using mechanistic modelling in ecology and evolution after the hackathon.
Outline:
In this session, we will:
1) introduce participants to what exactly are mechanistic models in ecology and evolution,
2) highlight broad issues of reproducibility, validation, sensitivity, and uncertainty quantification within mechanistic models,
3) provide a proposed framework for assessing models in terms of the FAIR principles and develop principles as a group to assessing mechanistic modelling studies specifically, and
4) apply these principles to a pilot study (time permitting).
We hope to eventually develop a publication or commentary piece as a result of the hackathon, and participants will be informed of the steps required to contribute to the project and be a co-author going forward after the hackathon.
Audience: Everyone – prior knowledge of mechanistic models is an asset but not required. Just arrive with a willingness to learn!

Program: Hackathon 5: Let’s expand the dataset of learned societies in ecology and evolutionary biology
Topic: We will expand the existing dataset of learned societies in ecology and evolutionary biology—currently focused mostly on international organizations—by adding a broad range of national-level societies from around the world, which are currently underrepresented. Once complete, this enhanced dataset will provide a foundation for future meta-research projects and support SORTEE’s efforts to engage with more learned societies. This hackathon will also offer structured networking opportunities to explore transparent methods for online data collection, and it will serve as a forum for generating ideas for future initiatives that connect learned societies with Open Science.
Outline: After a brief introduction, participants will collect and submit structured data on relevant societies through online forms, which will feed into a shared dataset. After the hackathon, we will acknowledge all contributors and coordinate asynchronous data cross-checking and gap-filling using shared online forms and spreadsheets. Collaboration and communication will be maintained through email, Slack, and Zoom as needed. Finalised dataset will be publicly deposited with a DOI, and we may also prepare a data manuscript for EcoEvoRxiv, with all eligible contributors listed as co-authors. This initiative builds on the SORTEE hackathons of 2022, 2023, and 2024, using the same framework to ensure equitable, productive, and enjoyable collaboration.
Audience: No specialist skills are required—this topic is accessible and relevant to researchers at all career stages worldwide. We particularly welcome participants with diverse linguistic backgrounds, as many local societies have an online presence only in non-English languages. This project offers a unique opportunity to showcase the diversity of learned societies from non-English-speaking countries and to build lasting connections between these societies and SORTEE.

Program: Unconference 5: How to start your own Code Club
Topic: This session explores how researchers at all levels (from bachelor students to faculty) can establish and grow code clubs within academic environments. The main goal is to foster peer learning and the adoption of practical coding skills directly linked to research needs. Participants will share experiences, tackle common challenges, and swap resources to build sustainable and inclusive code communities.
Outline: The session begins with brief introductions to surface participant backgrounds and coding motivations. Participants then collaboratively identify pressing questions and themes, which feed into an interactive discussion or breakout groups targeting the unique challenges of academic code clubs. The group reconvenes to swap favorite resources and compile ongoing community tools. The session closes with concrete action steps and networking opportunities to sustain momentum beyond the event.

Program: Unconference 6: Let’s DAG in – How Directed Acyclic Graphs can help Behavioural Ecology be more transparent
Topic: This session aims to demonstrate how Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) can clarify hypotheses, reveal hidden assumptions and guide better statistical modelling in the field of behavioural ecology. Participants will engage with real biological examples and learn the basic structures of DAGs, how DAGs help decide what to control for and how to communicate their research transparently through the use of their own DAGs. We will end the session by discussing whether and how using DAGs can help communicate our research, peer review and aid reproducibility.
Outline: In this interactive session, participants will first explore how biological assumptions can influence model choice by selecting from different linear regression models using a live poll, followed by a short discussion to unpack their reasoning. We will then introduce the fundamental concepts of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) and do an exercise with biological examples to let participants identify appropriate controls, collaborating in breakout groups. Causal DAGs can get complicated in practice, especially in our fields, and we will demonstrate this with an example to illustrate why DAGs can still be a useful tool in our studies. We will share insights from a review of 245 papers on DAG practices, highlighting best practices and challenges. The session will conclude with a structured discussion where participants share their opinions on DAGs through a series of questions and optional whiteboard activity - “Draw your own DAG”.
Audience: Everyone. Prerequisite: basic knowledge of linear regression models

Program: Unconference 7: How to think about hypothesis testing in ecology?
Facilitators: Gabriela Xavier-Quintais, Daniel Lakens, Tiago A. Marques
Topic: In this unconference, we will collectively consider the role that hypothesis testing should fulfil in ecological studies: observational/randomised studies, plant/animal studies, field/laboratory studies. This discussion will be based on the reflection that there are some specific constraints in ecology studies that could limit how hypothesis testing is used: constraints on sample sizes, difficulty in controlling variables, etc. Taking this into account, we will also discuss how researchers can collectively solve the widespread problem of the misuse of hypothesis testing in scientific research in ecology.
Outline:
- In the first 10 minutes, a brief overview of the theme and purpose of the unconference will be provided, accompanied by some results from a meta-scientific study in ecology. </br>
- Then, some questions will be presented, one by one, which the audience will be asked to discuss and answer together.</br>
- In the last 5/10 minutes, there will be an overview of what has been discussed, with the aim of consolidating what should be done (according to our discussion) in the near future to mitigate the problems described. The result of this dynamic discussion will be written up and shared with the SORTEE community a few days after the event, allowing everyone to read it and continue to reflect on it (two documents will be created: one static and one editable) — an important ongoing discussion.
